chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from al-Amriki ibn Ali, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who performed Tawaf around the House while in a state of Janabah (major ritual impurity), and he remembered [his impurity] while he was in the Tawaf, so he said: 'He breaks his Tawaf and does not count anything of what he has performed [as valid].'
And I asked him about a man who performed Tawaf and then remembered that he was upon [a state of] non-Wudu (minor ritual impurity), he said: 'He breaks his Tawaf and does not count it [as valid].'

And these narrations, although they are absolute or most of them indicate that he repeats the Tawaf, we have restricted them to the Tawaf of the Fard (obligatory) because of what we previously presented from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Muslim, that he distinguished the ruling of the two Tawafs: the Tawaf of the Fard and the Tawaf of the Sunnah, and the ruling of the detailed [text] upon the general [text] is more preferable.
And that is increased in clarification by what he narrated:
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on Tawaf if one remembers they are in a state of Janabah or without Wudu during the circumambulation?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi clarifies that the absolute rulings on invalidating Tawaf due to impurity apply specifically to the obligatory (Fard) circumambation, distinguishing it from voluntary (Sunnah) Tawaf based on the principle that specific texts override general ones. This distinction highlights the rigorous purity requirements for the primary pillar of Hajj and Umrah, ensuring the validity of the core ritual act.
